title: Ch. 8 Lecture Slides
description: Original exam-style questions from Dr. Letendre's Chapter 8 slides and Week 8 lecture: AE model, MPC/MPS, 45°-line equilibrium, the multiplier, the algebra, and deriving AD.

table25.title: Macroeconomic equilibrium: a numerical example
table25.body: Values are in trillions of 2017 dollars. Planned investment, government purchases and net exports are constant at every level of GDP.

questions.prompt: The aggregate expenditure model is a short-run macroeconomic model that explains how total spending determines real GDP, assuming that…

options.text: the price level adjusts instantly to clear the goods market
the price level is constant
real GDP always equals potential GDP
the interest rate is zero

questions.explanation: Slide 3: it is a short-run model in which the **price level is constant**. Because prices cannot adjust, **unplanned inventory changes** (not prices) push the economy to equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Planned investment is $150 billion and firms experience an unplanned increase in inventories of $40 billion. Actual investment is…

options.text: $110 billion
$150 billion
$190 billion (actual = planned + unplanned change in inventories)
$40 billion

questions.explanation: Slide 4: **actual investment = planned investment + unplanned change in inventories** = 150 + 40 = 190. The AE model uses planned investment, so AE differs slightly from GDP.

questions.prompt: In the AE model, macroeconomic equilibrium occurs when…

options.text: planned aggregate expenditure equals potential GDP
the price level equals its long-run value
actual investment equals zero
planned aggregate expenditure equals GDP, so unplanned inventory change is zero

questions.explanation: Equilibrium: **C + I<sub>p</sub> + G + NX = GDP**. Then firms sell exactly what they expected and have no reason to change production.

questions.prompt: Using the table, what is equilibrium real GDP (trillions of 2017 dollars)?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is where planned AE = GDP. At Y = 3.00: AE = 2.75 + 0.15 + 0.15 − 0.05 = 3.00 = Y, and unplanned inventory investment is 0. Equilibrium GDP = **$3.0 trillion**.

questions.prompt: Using the table, if real GDP is $3.5 trillion, by how much (trillions) do inventories change unexpectedly? (Enter a negative number for a decrease.)
questions.explanation: Unplanned inventory investment = Y − AE = 3.50 − 3.25 = **+0.25**. GDP is above AE, so inventories pile up and firms cut production.

questions.prompt: Using the table, if real GDP is currently $2.0 trillion, what happens next?

options.text: AE ($2.50 trillion) exceeds GDP, inventories fall unexpectedly by $0.50 trillion, so firms raise production and GDP rises
AE is below GDP, inventories rise unexpectedly, so firms raise production
Prices fall until AE equals GDP
Nothing; any level of GDP is an equilibrium in the short run

questions.explanation: At Y = 2.0, AE = 2.50 > Y, so unplanned inventory investment is −0.50. Firms see shelves emptying and **increase output** until GDP reaches 3.0. Prices don't adjust because they are assumed constant.

questions.prompt: Consumption rises from $750 to $2,250 (billions) when real GDP rises from $1,000 to $3,000 (net taxes constant). What is the MPC?
questions.explanation: MPC = ΔC/ΔY = (2,250 − 750)/(3,000 − 1,000) = 1,500/2,000 = **0.75**. With constant net taxes, it is also the slope of C against GDP.

questions.prompt: Using the slides' estimate MPC = 0.764, by how many dollars would consumption rise if disposable income rises by $10,000?
Suppose MPC = 0.8. If national income rises by $500 (taxes constant), by how much does saving rise?
Which of the following causes a movement along the consumption function rather than a shift of it?

options.text: A rise in household wealth
A change in current disposable income
A change in expected future income
A change in real interest rates

questions.explanation: Current disposable income is the variable on the axis, so changing it moves you **along** the line (slope = MPC). Wealth, expectations, the price level and interest rates **shift** the function.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would most likely increase planned investment?

options.text: A rise in the real interest rate
An increase in corporate taxes
Firms become optimistic about future profitability
A fall in firms' cash flow

questions.explanation: Slide 17: investment rises with **expected future profits**, lower real interest rates, lower corporate taxes and stronger cash flow. The other three all lower it.

questions.prompt: A stronger Canadian dollar will most likely…

options.text: raise net exports, since Canadian goods become cheaper abroad
raise net exports, since imports become more expensive
have no effect on net exports
lower net exports, since imports become cheaper and exports more expensive

questions.explanation: A stronger dollar makes **imports cheaper and exports more expensive**, so exports fall, imports rise and NX decreases. Faster Canadian growth also lowers NX because it raises imports.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is counted in government purchases (G)?

options.text: A province buying a new highway interchange
Employment insurance payments to the unemployed
Old age pension payments to retirees
Interest paid on the government debt

questions.explanation: G covers spending on **goods and services**, including government investment (roads, buildings). **Transfer payments** are excluded because no good or service is received in return.

questions.prompt: If MPC = 0.75, what is the value of the multiplier?
Because of optimism about the profits AI will produce, firms raise planned investment by $250 billion. If MPC = 0.5, by how much (billions) does equilibrium GDP increase?
questions.explanation: Multiplier = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2. ΔY = 2 × 250 = **$500 billion**: the first-round $250 plus $125 + $62.5 + … of induced consumption.

questions.prompt: Total change in GDP = $250(1 + MPC + MPC² + MPC³ + …). Why does the series contain powers of the MPC?

options.text: Because the MPC rises in each round
Each round of income is partly re-spent: a fraction MPC of every dollar of new income becomes the next round's consumption spending
Because each round is taxed at the MPC
Because planned investment keeps rising by the MPC each round

questions.explanation: The initial $250 of spending becomes income; households spend MPC × 250, which becomes income again, and so on. The sum of the geometric series is **250/(1 − MPC)**.

questions.prompt: C = 100 + 0.8Y, I<sub>p</sub> = 125, G = 125, NX = −30. Find equilibrium real GDP.
Using the same model (C = 100 + 0.8Y, I<sub>p</sub> = 125, G = 125, NX = −30), what is the unplanned change in inventories if real GDP is 1,400? (Negative = decrease.)
questions.explanation: AE = 100 + 0.8(1,400) + 125 + 125 − 30 = 100 + 1,120 + 220 = 1,440. Unplanned inventory change = Y − AE = 1,400 − 1,440 = **−40**. Since GDP is below the equilibrium of 1,600, inventories fall and output rises.

questions.prompt: In the same model (equilibrium Y = 1,600), government purchases rise from 125 to 145. What is the new equilibrium real GDP?
C̄ = 150, MPC = 0.75, I<sub>p</sub> = 100, G = 120, NX = −20. Using Equilibrium GDP = autonomous expenditure × multiplier, find equilibrium GDP.
MPC = 0.6. Net exports fall by $80 billion because of a trade war. By how much (billions) does equilibrium GDP change? (Enter a negative number for a decrease.)
questions.explanation: Multiplier = 1/(1 − 0.6) = 2.5. ΔY = 2.5 × (−80) = **−$200 billion**. The multiplier works in both directions.

questions.prompt: Starting from equilibrium at potential GDP, US policy reduces Canadian exports. On the 45°-line diagram, what happens?

options.text: The AE line shifts up; the new equilibrium is above potential GDP and the economy overheats
The 45° line shifts down; equilibrium stays at potential GDP
The AE line shifts down; the new equilibrium is below potential GDP, firms operate below normal capacity and unemployment exceeds the natural rate
The AE line pivots so that its slope (MPC) falls, with no change in the intercept

questions.explanation: A fall in NX is a fall in autonomous expenditure, so the **AE line shifts down** and the intersection with the 45° line moves left, below potential GDP. Cyclical unemployment appears. The 45° line never moves.

questions.prompt: Potential GDP is best described as…

options.text: the maximum output the economy could ever produce
the level of real GDP where AE is maximized
the level of GDP that firms plan to produce in a recession
real GDP when firms operate at normal capacity with a normal workforce, i.e. full employment with zero cyclical unemployment

questions.explanation: Slide 26: potential GDP reflects **sustainable** production, not maximum possible output; at potential GDP cyclical unemployment is zero. It grows with labour, capital and technology.

questions.prompt: Households become worried and all try to save more. According to the slides, in the short run…

options.text: AE and real GDP fall; incomes drop, so households may end up no better off, and the economy can enter a recession
AE and real GDP rise because higher saving funds investment immediately
Real GDP is unchanged because saving equals investment by definition
Only the price level changes

questions.explanation: The **paradox of thrift**: saving more is good for long-run growth (it funds investment), but in the short run lower consumption cuts sales, production and jobs, so GDP falls.

questions.prompt: The simple multiplier formula 1/(1 − MPC) tends to overstate the effect on GDP because it ignores…

options.text: the MPC, which is already in the formula
imports, inflation, interest rates and taxes, which dampen the overall effect
the fact that government purchases are autonomous
the fact that investment is planned

questions.explanation: Slide 32: imports, taxes, interest-rate increases and price-level increases all reduce the size of the real-world multiplier.

questions.prompt: Each point on the aggregate demand curve corresponds to…

options.text: a point on the 45° line for a fixed real GDP
a level of potential GDP
an equilibrium of the Keynesian cross (45°-line) diagram for a given price level
the intersection of AE with the vertical axis

questions.explanation: Slide 34: to derive AD we find how a change in P changes the AE line and the resulting equilibrium. Each (P, equilibrium Y) pair is a point on AD.

questions.topic: Price level and the AE line
questions.prompt: The price level rises (P₁ to P₃). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The AE line shifts up; equilibrium GDP rises: a movement along the AD curve
The AE line shifts down; this shifts the AD curve to the left
The AE line does not move; the AD curve shifts left
The AE line shifts down (C, I<sub>p</sub> and NX fall at every GDP); equilibrium GDP falls: a movement up along the AD curve

questions.explanation: Higher P lowers real wealth (C), raises interest rates (I<sub>p</sub>) and raises Canadian prices relative to foreign (NX). The AE line **shifts**, but the change in P is a **movement along AD**, not a shift of AD. A trap on the test.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is NOT one of the slides' reasons why a higher price level lowers planned aggregate expenditure?

options.text: Government purchases are cut automatically whenever prices rise
Real household wealth falls, lowering consumption
Canadian goods become more expensive relative to foreign goods, lowering net exports
Money demand rises, interest rates rise and planned investment falls

questions.explanation: The three channels are consumption (wealth), net exports (relative prices) and investment (interest rates). G is set by policy and is not tied to the price level.

questions.prompt: The economy is in equilibrium at E₁. Optimistic firms raise planned investment (an autonomous increase). Draw the new aggregate expenditure line AE₂ and mark the new equilibrium E₂.
questions.explanation: Higher planned investment is an **autonomous** increase, so the whole AE line shifts **up** (parallel; the slope is still the MPC). The new equilibrium is where AE₂ crosses the 45° line: further up and to the right, and GDP rises by **more** than the initial increase in investment (the multiplier).

questions.prompt: The economy starts in equilibrium at potential GDP (E₁). US policy then reduces Canadian exports. Draw the new AE line AE₂ and mark the new equilibrium E₂.
questions.explanation: A fall in NX is a fall in autonomous expenditure: the AE line shifts **down**. The new equilibrium is where AE₂ crosses the 45° line, **to the left of potential GDP**: firms operate below normal capacity and unemployment exceeds the natural rate (a recession).

questions.prompt: At price level P₁ the quantity of real GDP demanded is 3.0 (point A). When the price level falls to P₂, the AE line shifts up and GDP demanded rises to 3.5 (point B). Draw the aggregate demand curve through A and B.
questions.explanation: Each point on AD is an equilibrium from the Keynesian cross for one price level. A lower P shifts AE up and raises equilibrium GDP from 3.0 to 3.5, so AD is **downward sloping**: it passes through A and B. The change in P is a movement **along** AD.
